paragraphs: But in the drawing-room the conversation was already over. Katerina Ivanovna was very excited, though she looked resolute. Just as Alyosha and Madame Hohlakov came in, Ivan Fyodorovitch stood up to say goodbye. His face was rather pale, and Alyosha looked at him anxiously. This moment was going to settle a doubt, a tormenting riddle that had haunted Alyosha for some time. Over the past month, several people had hinted to him that his brother Ivan was in love with Katerina Ivanovna and, what was more, meant “to carry her off” from Dmitri. Until quite recently the idea had seemed monstrous to Alyosha, though it worried him terribly. He loved both his brothers and dreaded a rivalry between them. Meanwhile, Dmitri had said outright the day before that he was glad Ivan was his rival, and that it was a great help to him, Dmitri. How did it help him? To marry Grushenka? But Alyosha thought that the worst thing possible. Besides all this, Alyosha had believed without question, until the evening before, that Katerina Ivanovna loved Dmitri steadily and passionately; but he had believed it only until the evening before. He had also imagined that she was incapable of loving a man like Ivan, and that she did love Dmitri, and loved him just as he was, however strange such a passion might be.

But during yesterday’s scene with Grushenka another idea had struck him. The word “lacerating,” which Madame Hohlakov had just used, nearly made him jump. Half awake toward daybreak that night, he had cried out “Laceration, laceration,” probably about his dream. He had dreamed all night of the previous day’s scene at Katerina Ivanovna’s. Now he was struck by Madame Hohlakov’s blunt and persistent claim that Katerina Ivanovna was in love with Ivan, and was only deceiving herself through some sort of pose, out of “self-laceration,” tormenting herself with a pretended love for Dmitri from some imagined duty of gratitude. “Yes,” he thought, “perhaps the whole truth lies in those words.” But in that case, where did that leave Ivan? Alyosha felt instinctively that a character like Katerina Ivanovna’s had to dominate, and that she could dominate only someone like Dmitri, never a man like Ivan. Dmitri might in the end submit to her domination “to his own happiness” (which was what Alyosha would have wanted), but Ivan—no, Ivan could not submit to her, and submission would not make him happy. Alyosha could not help believing that of Ivan. And now all these doubts and reflections flitted through his mind as he entered the drawing-room. Another thought forced itself on him too: “What if she loved neither of them—neither Ivan nor Dmitri?”

It must be said that Alyosha felt rather ashamed of his own thoughts, and blamed himself whenever they kept coming back to him over the past month. “What do I know about love and women, and how can I decide such questions?” he thought reproachfully, after such doubts and guesses. And yet it was impossible not to think about it. He felt instinctively that this rivalry was of immense importance in his brothers’ lives and that a great deal depended on it.

“One reptile will devour the other,” Ivan had declared the day before, speaking in anger of his father and Dmitri. So Ivan looked on Dmitri as a reptile, and perhaps had done so for a long time. Perhaps ever since he had known Katerina Ivanovna? That phrase had, of course, slipped out of Ivan yesterday without his meaning it, but that only made it more important. If he felt like that, what chance was there of peace? Were there not, on the contrary, new grounds for hatred and hostility in their family? And which of them was Alyosha to side with? And what was he to wish for each of them? He loved them both, but what could he wish for either of them amid these conflicting interests? He might lose his way completely in this maze, and Alyosha’s heart could not bear uncertainty, because his love was always active. He was incapable of passive love. If he loved someone, he set to work at once to help him. And to do that he had to know what he was aiming at; he had to know for certain what was best for each of them, and once he had found that out, it was natural for him to help them both. But instead of a definite aim, he found nothing but uncertainty and bewilderment on all sides. “It was lacerating,” as had just been said. But what could he understand even in this “laceration”? He did not understand the first word in this bewildering maze.

Seeing Alyosha, Katerina Ivanovna said quickly and joyfully to Ivan, who had already stood up to go, “One minute! Stay one more minute! I want to hear the opinion of this person here, whom I trust absolutely. Don’t go away,” she added, turning to Madame Hohlakov. She made Alyosha sit down beside her, and Madame Hohlakov sat opposite, next to Ivan.

“You are all my friends here, all I have in the world, my dear friends,” she began warmly, in a voice that shook with real tears of suffering, and Alyosha’s heart warmed to her at once. “Alexey Fyodorovitch, you were a witness yesterday of that abominable scene, and you saw what I did. You didn’t see it, Ivan Fyodorovitch; he did. What he thought of me yesterday I don’t know. I only know one thing: if it happened again today, this minute, I would express the same feelings again as yesterday—the same feelings, the same words, the same actions. You remember my actions, Alexey Fyodorovitch; you stopped me in one of them” ... (as she said that, she flushed and her eyes shone). “I have to tell you that I can’t get over it. Listen, Alexey Fyodorovitch. I don’t even know whether I still love _him_. I feel _pity_ for him, and that is a poor sign of love. If I loved him, if I still loved him, perhaps I wouldn’t be sorry for him now, but would hate him.”
Her voice shook, and tears glittered on her eyelashes. Alyosha shuddered inwardly. “That girl is truthful and sincere,” he thought, “and she doesn’t love Dmitri any more.”
“That’s true, that’s true,” cried Madame Hohlakov.

“Wait, dear. I haven’t told you the main thing, the final decision I came to during the night. I feel that my decision may be a terrible one—for me, but I foresee that nothing will make me change it—nothing. It will be so all my life. My dear, kind, ever-faithful and generous adviser, the one friend I have in the world, Ivan Fyodorovitch, who sees so deeply into the heart, approves and commends my decision. He knows it.”
“Yes, I approve of it,” Ivan agreed, in a low but firm voice.

“But I would like Alyosha, too (Ah! Alexey Fyodorovitch, forgive me for calling you simply Alyosha), I would like Alexey Fyodorovitch, too, to tell me in front of my two friends whether I am right. I feel instinctively that you, Alyosha, my dear brother (for you are a dear brother to me),” she said again, rapturously, taking his cold hand in her hot one, “I foresee that your decision, your approval, will bring me peace, in spite of all my suffering, for after your words I shall be calm and submit—I feel that.”

“I don’t know what you are asking me,” said Alyosha, flushing. “I only know that I love you and at this moment wish for your happiness more than my own!... But I know nothing about such matters,” something made him add hurriedly.

“In such matters, Alexey Fyodorovitch, in such matters, the main thing is honor and duty and something higher—I don’t know what—but perhaps higher even than duty. I feel this irresistible feeling in my heart, and it compels me irresistibly. But it can all be put in two words. I have already decided that even if he marries that—creature,” she began solemnly, “whom I never, never can forgive, _even then I will not abandon him_. From now on I will never, never abandon him!” she cried, breaking into a sort of pale, hysterical ecstasy. “Not that I would run after him constantly, get in his way and trouble him. Oh, no! I will go away to another town—wherever you like—but I will watch over him all my life—I will watch over him all my life without ceasing. When he becomes unhappy with that woman, and that is bound to happen very soon, let him come to me and he will find a friend, a sister.... Only a sister, of course, and so for ever; but he will learn at least that that sister really is his sister, who loves him and has sacrificed her whole life to him. I will get my way. I will insist that he know me and confide in me completely, without holding anything back,” she cried, in a sort of frenzy. “I will be a god to whom he can pray—and that, at least, he owes me for his treachery and for what I suffered yesterday because of him. And let him see that all my life I will be true to him and to the promise I gave him, in spite of his being untrue and betraying me. I will—I will become nothing but a means to his happiness, or—how shall I say?—an instrument, a machine for his happiness, and that for my whole life, my whole life, and let him see that all his life! That’s my decision. Ivan Fyodorovitch fully approves of me.”

She was out of breath. She had perhaps meant to put her idea with more dignity, skill and naturalness, but her speech was too hurried and crude. It was full of youthful impulsiveness, it showed that she was still smarting from yesterday’s insult, and that her pride demanded satisfaction. She felt this herself. Her face suddenly darkened, and an unpleasant look came into her eyes. Alyosha saw it at once and felt a pang of sympathy. His brother Ivan made it worse by adding:

“I’ve only given my own view,” he said. “From anyone else, this would have seemed affected and overstrained, but from you—no. Any other woman would have been wrong, but you are right. I don’t know how to explain it, but I can see that you are absolutely genuine and, therefore, you are right.”

“But that’s only for the moment. And what does this moment amount to? Nothing but yesterday’s insult.” Madame Hohlakov obviously had not meant to interfere, but she could not hold back this very just remark.

“Quite so, quite so,” cried Ivan, with peculiar eagerness, plainly annoyed at being interrupted, “in anyone else this moment would be due only to yesterday’s impression and would be only a moment. But with Katerina Ivanovna’s character, that moment will last all her life. What for anyone else would be only a promise is for her an everlasting, burdensome, perhaps grim, but unflagging duty. And she will be sustained by the feeling that this duty is being fulfilled. Your life, Katerina Ivanovna, will from now on be spent in painful brooding over your own feelings, your own heroism, and your own suffering; but in the end that suffering will soften and will turn into a sweet contemplation of the fulfillment of a bold and proud design. Yes, proud it certainly is, and desperate in any case, but a triumph for you. And the awareness of it will at last be a source of complete satisfaction and will make you resigned to everything else.”
This was said unmistakably with some malice and plainly on purpose; perhaps he did not even want to hide that he spoke ironically and on purpose.
“Oh dear, how mistaken it all is!” Madame Hohlakov cried again.
“Alexey Fyodorovitch, you speak. I want so dreadfully to know what you will say!” cried Katerina Ivanovna, and burst into tears. Alyosha got up from the sofa.

“It’s nothing, nothing!” she went on through her tears. “I’m upset, I didn’t sleep last night. But beside two such friends as you and your brother I still feel strong—for I know—you two will never desert me.”
“Unfortunately I have to go back to Moscow—perhaps tomorrow—and leave you for a long time—And, unfortunately, it can’t be helped,” Ivan said suddenly.

“Tomorrow—to Moscow!” her face was suddenly twisted; “but—but, good heavens, how fortunate!” she cried in a voice suddenly changed. In one instant there was no trace left of her tears. She went through an instant transformation, which amazed Alyosha. Instead of a poor, insulted girl, weeping in a kind of “laceration,” he saw a woman completely self-possessed and even exceedingly pleased, as though something agreeable had just happened.

“Oh, not fortunate that I am losing you, of course not,” she corrected herself suddenly, with a charming society smile. “A friend like you could not think that. I am only too unhappy at losing you.” She rushed impulsively at Ivan, and seizing both his hands, pressed them warmly. “But what is fortunate is that in Moscow you will be able to see auntie and Agafya and tell them all the horror of my present position. You can speak with complete openness to Agafya, but spare dear auntie. You will know how to do that. You can’t imagine how wretched I was yesterday and this morning, wondering how I could write them that dreadful letter—for one can never tell such things in a letter.... Now it will be easy for me to write, for you will see them and explain everything. Oh, how glad I am! But I am glad only of that, believe me. Of course, no one can take your place.... I will run and write the letter at once,” she finished suddenly, and took a step as though to leave the room.
